items.text:
US adds Megaspeed, firm at centre of Nvidia scandal, to export control list
Bureau of Security and Industry adds Singapore-based firm and six other entities to export control list.
The United States government has added the Singapore-based company at the centre of the spying claims surrounding Nvidia to its trade blacklist.
The Bureau of Security and Industry (BIS) placed Megaspeed International and six other firms on entity list on Monday, hours after Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia as CEO in a stunning comeback that sent tech stocks soaring.
Megaspeed and the six other entities were determined to be “acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States,” BIS said in a filing to the Federal Register.
The designations mean that any company or person seeking to ship advanced US technology, such as Nvidia top-end graphics processing units (GPUs) used to power AI, to the firms first must obtain an export licence.
The other six entities added to the list are MSFusion, PT Megaspeed International, and Speedmatrix, based in Malaysia; Apex Enterprise Solutions and Swiftdata, based in Singapore; and Megaspeed, based in Thailand.
More to follow…

items.summary:
What could Democrats do with their expanding congressional majority?

items.text:
What could Democrats do with their expanding congressional majority?
The Democratic Party is debating how best to use its large margin of victory in the US midterm elections.
The Democratic Party has continued to expand its already sizeable majorities in the United States Congress as counting concludes in the final races of the 2026 midterm elections.
As of Monday, the Democrats hold a 258-seat majority in the 435-member House of Representatives. Four races remain uncalled.
All the races have been decided, meanwhile, for the Senate, where Democrats gained a 56-seat majority out of 100 total seats.
Flipping both chambers gives the party a strong hand to shape legislation during the last two years of Trump’s term in office.
How might the Democrats approach their role in government once the new Congress is sworn in on January 3? Find out in this quick explainer.
What do the results say?
The midterm results give Democrats their largest House majority since 1992 and their largest Senate majority in more than a decade. Republicans, meanwhile, saw their tally in the House drop to 173 seats, their lowest figure in years.
The vote also served as a firm rebuke of Trump’s second term as president, with voters venting their frustration over cost-of-living issues, the US-Israel war on Iran, aggressive immigration raids and corruption.
Democratic victories also extended well beyond traditional left-wing strongholds, with candidates racking up wins in Republican-led states such as Texas, Mississippi and South Carolina.
Which races remain?
Four House seats have yet to be called: one in Minnesota, one in Tennessee, and two in Louisiana that will be settled by a run-off on December 12.
Those races could see the Democrats further expand their majority in the House. The final count is now a question of just how large the party’s majority will be.
What will Democrats do with their majority?
Democrats have long pledged to use any congressional majorities they win as a check on Trump’s agenda.
But the scale of their success in the 2026 midterms has prompted discussion about embracing a more ambitious legislative agenda.
In the House of Representatives, Democrats have outlined a 100-day agenda that includes potentially reversing tax cuts that largely benefit wealthy earners and restoring healthcare subsidies that expired under Trump.
Lawmakers have also said that they will act to end the war on Iran, although divisions remain within the party over how to rein in Trump’s military actions. Under the US Constitution, Congress alone can authorise military operations.
Progressives have accused the party’s moderate wing of playing down expectations of firm steps to end the war, including cutting off funding.
Democrats have also pledged to use their newfound position to exercise oversight over the executive branch by launching probes and issuing subpoenas.
On Monday, for example, House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said that a Democrat-led Congress would conduct a “swift, thorough, and wide-ranging” investigation into the actions of the chip manufacturer Nvidia.
He also said it would delve into the “corrupt abuse of power” by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
In the Senate, Democrats have also threatened to block Trump’s nominees for high-level government positions, which require the chamber’s confirmation.
What role will Trump play?
While Democrats will hold substantial majorities in both chambers of Congress, Trump will retain the power to veto legislation.
Some lawmakers, however, have tried to persuade the president that he could benefit from working with Democrats after his party’s stark defeat in the midterms.
Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, for example, has shared a series of tongue-in-cheek social media posts suggesting that a universal healthcare programme — a long-term progressive goal — could be named after the president in a bid to win his support.
“Donald, this is on the table,” El-Sayed said in a social media post showing a card for a hypothetical health insurance programme titled “Trumpcare”. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”
Could Trump work with the Democrats?
There is little evidence, however, to suggest that Trump is planning a political pivot after the midterms.
Within a week of the vote, for instance, Trump named Stephen Miller — one of the architects of his hardline policies on immigration — as White House chief of staff.
The staffing shake-up was seen as a doubling-down on right-wing policy priorities.
While Trump has, at times, suggested that he could cooperate with Democratic lawmakers, he has also promised to use his veto power aggressively.
He has also taken to social media to disparage Chuck Schumer, who is currently seeking to become the next Senate majority leader, a position he previously held from 2021 to 2025.
“It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Sunday.
“He failed badly as ‘Leader’ once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again.”
Trump’s White House has also threatened to take action if Democrats aggressively use their oversight powers in Congress.
“Members of the new Congress have evinced a clear intent to transgress” the constitutional limits of their power, White House counsel Will Scharf wrote in a letter on November 9, gesturing to the prospect of congressional investigations.

items.title: Zelensky urges four-way peace talks with Russia, Europe and US 'as soon as possible'
items.summary:
Zelensky urges four-way peace talks with Russia, Europe and US 'as soon as possible'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is calling for a new round of negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia, the United States and European leaders, saying Kyiv is ready to meet as early as Tuesday.
Ukrainian Presid
items.text:
Zelensky urges four-way peace talks with Russia, Europe and US 'as soon as possible'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is calling for a new round of negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia, the United States and European leaders, saying Kyiv is ready to meet as early as Tuesday.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday called for new negotiations with Russia involving European leaders to be held as soon as possible and repeated a plea for his country to join the NATO alliance.
Zelensky, speaking by video to a gathering of lawmakers from NATO countries in Berlin, welcomed the latest push for peace talks with Moscow.
"We must do everything to make sure that the four-party meeting -- Ukraine, Europe, America and Russia -- happens as soon as possible. We are ready to do this. Literally tomorrow," Zelensky said.
"We have heard from our partners that they want to try to make it happen before Christmas. We hope it happens sooner."
European governments have been excluded from past discussions and their push to join talks has gained prominence in recent weeks.
Zelensky, whose country has been battling a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022, has repeatedly called for a path to full membership in NATO -- and not simply receiving security guarantees from alliance countries.
He argued that Ukraine's combat experience, innovative defence industry and large military would all benefit other allies.
"NATO is the answer -- and with a strong Ukrainian army, NATO itself is guaranteed to be stronger," Zelensky told the Berlin gathering.
A number of NATO leaders have expressed hesitation about bringing Ukraine into the alliance.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, speaking after Zelensky at the same event on Monday, underscored the alliance's support for Ukraine but noted that joining would require unanimous support.
"Not all NATO allies agree at this moment (on) letting Ukraine become a member," Rutte said, though he also firmly rejected the idea that outside powers like Russia could dictate who joins the alliance.
During a gathering of Ukrainian supporters in Berlin last week, US envoy Jared Kushner said that Washington might consider offering Ukraine a security guarantee similar to that provided under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty as part of a peace settlement.
But in his remarks on Monday, Zelensky said major questions remain about how such guarantees would work without a full NATO commitment.
"Which countries will support Ukraine if Ukraine is attacked again? What exactly will our partners do in response? Which troops will be stationed on our territory in advance? How much will all this cost? And will it really work?
"All of this is not easy and so far we have not heard clear specific answers," Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian leader also repeated a call for NATO countries to provide more air defence weapons, urging them to empty their stockpiles to allow Ukraine to repel Russian airstrikes.
"Missiles that can stop Russian ballistic missiles should not be sitting in warehouses collecting dust," he said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.text:
Trump calls to ‘expedite’ US federal executions, blasts Gavin Newsom
The US president used his podium to attack the California governor for a decision to commute 548 death sentences.
United States President Donald Trump has reaffirmed his support for the death penalty in an event that doubled as a platform to attack one of his most visible critics, California Governor Gavin Newsom.
On Monday, Trump spoke at the Department of Justice in Washington, DC, where he was joined by the families of crime victims and his attorney general, Todd Blanche.
“The ultimate crimes deserve the ultimate punishment,” Trump said of the death penalty, calling it a cornerstone of “ virtually every society throughout history, at least every successful society”.
“Under the Trump administration, we are bringing it back, and we will not stop in our pursuit of justice. We will not yield.”
He concluded the appearance by signing a presidential directive ordering the Department of Justice to seek the death penalty in murder cases involving children, rape and human trafficking.
The directive also pushes for the attorney general to “expedite” executions for those on federal death row.
As part of his speech, Trump called on Congress to pass the Just Punishment for Murder Act, a bill sponsored by Republican Representative Brandon Gill, which the president said would “strengthen the death penalty in America”.
But he dedicated much of his remarks to slamming Newsom, a Democrat widely seen as a possible contender for the 2028 presidential race.
Newsom’s second term as governor will end on January 4. Under California term limits, he was ineligible to run again in the 2026 midterm elections.
Still, the governor and former San Francisco mayor has carved a national profile for himself as a proxy for Democrats during high-stakes political campaigns — and as a critic of Trump.
Trump, however, zeroed in on one of Newsom’s final major actions while in office: commuting the sentences of those on California’s death row.
On November 5, two days after the midterms, Newsom announced that the 548 people sentenced to death in California would instead be sentenced to life without the possibility of parole.
He described the action as an extension of the moratorium on executions he put in place after taking office in 2019.
“I could not remain true to my values and oversee the killing of people with death warrants in California,” he wrote in an open letter.
He nevertheless denounced the harm the 548 people had caused.
“Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die,” Newsom wrote. “But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them.”
He called on Californians to let the 548 people “die in obscurity” while remembering their victims.
Trump, however, framed the mass commutation as an effort to help “evil monsters” escape justice.
“This afternoon, we come together to stand against the travesty and to wrap our arms around the families of victims who were so cruelly betrayed by bad government and our political system,” Trump said.
The president proceeded to launch barbs at Newsom, calling him “ a terrible governor” who “ stole away the only closure” the victims’ families “might ever have”.
He then invited several family members on stage to denounce Newsom’s decision.
“ You took the only justice we had and left families feeling abandoned by the state that promised to protect us,” Sandra Friend, the mother of eight-year-old murder victim Michael Lyons, said in her remarks, directed at Newsom.
In anticipation of Monday’s news conference, Newsom also released statements from families that supported his choice.
“When victims are this divided, the death penalty shouldn’t be the answer. Victims deserve so much more than a promise of justice through vengeance,” Jess Nichol, the sister of murder victim Polly Klaas, said in one of the statements.
“They deserve counselling, medical care, financial support, and a justice system that helps them heal. I want something better for survivors: real, tangible support.”
The tit-for-tat between Newsom and Trump comes as support for the death penalty has slumped in recent years.
A November poll released by the research firm Gallup found that 49 percent of US adults support the death penalty, the lowest rate since 1971.
Opponents of the death penalty have frequently pointed to the prevalence of botched executions and the possibility that innocent people may be executed.
The Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit, has found that approximately 202 people formerly on death row were later found to be wrongfully convicted. The exoneration rate, it said, was one for every eight people executed in the US.
Death penalty cases also typically tend to result in longer court battles and higher costs.
Before Newsom’s mass commutation, California reportedly had the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere, representing roughly a quarter of the country’s death sentences.
Newsom’s successor, Governor-elect Xavier Becerra, has pledged to continue the death penalty moratorium once sworn in.
But that policy puts California at odds with a push under Trump to embrace the death penalty and expand execution methods.
Upon taking office for a second term on January 20, 2025, Trump signed the first of several executive orders aimed at “restoring the death penalty”.
He pushed to have execution be the de facto punishment for the murder of law enforcement officers, as well as for murder cases where undocumented immigrants are the defendants.
In April, the Trump administration also said it would prioritise the use of the death penalty by expanding the acceptable methods for federal execution, including firing squads.
In October, Trump’s Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that one execution by firing squad — that of the Fort Hood shooter, Nidal Hasan — would be livestreamed to the public, prompting backlash.
Trump later walked back the announcement, amid reports that he did not realise Hassan

items.text:
Borno school enrolment nearly doubles after years of conflict
Despite rising enrolment, violence, displacement and poverty keep children out of school in northeastern state.
Maiduguri, Nigeria – During years of Boko Haram violence, Maryam Umar’s school in Baga, a town in northeastern Nigeria’s Borno State, was forced to close as violence displaced families and disrupted education across the region.
The closure of the Higher Islamic College in Baga in the Kukawa Local Government Area was part of a wider crisis that deprived thousands of children of regular schooling.
With educational activities now resuming, Umar, a teacher, welcomed efforts to reopen schools and provide learning materials, telling Al Jazeera that the interventions were helping restore education in communities devastated by years of conflict.
Across Borno, authorities said school enrolment has risen sharply as damaged classrooms are repaired and families are encouraged to send their children back to school.
Enrolment in public and private schools reached 1,418,279 learners in 2025, up from 766,551 during the 2017-2018 academic session, according to the state government.
Yet officials estimated that almost 800,000 children remain out of school, highlighting the challenges facing a state where more than a decade of conflict has displaced communities and devastated public services.
The figures suggest progress in expanding access but reveal little about regular attendance, teaching quality or whether children who have missed years of education are catching up.
Rebuilding after years of violence
Borno has been at the centre of Boko Haram violence since the armed group launched its campaign in northeastern Nigeria in 2009.
Schools were among the institutions affected as attacks, displacement and a prolonged lack of security forced families to abandon their homes. In some communities, education became impossible as classrooms closed and teachers and pupils fled.
The state government has made school reconstruction a priority, building new facilities and rehabilitating classrooms damaged by conflict and flooding.
“In response, our administration has constructed 104 new schools and rehabilitated 2,931 classrooms and related facilities,” Governor Babagana Umara Zulum said during the commissioning of educational projects in Maiduguri in March.
According to the governor, the estimated number of out-of-school children has fallen from about 2.2 million at the height of the crisis to fewer than 800,000.
Borno Commissioner for Education, Science, Technology and Innovation Lawan Abba Wakilbe said the increase in enrolment reflects renewed confidence among parents.
But increased enrolment does not necessarily mean children are attending regularly or receiving the support they need after years of disrupted learning.
The available figures also provide little indication of whether the supply of qualified teachers and learning materials has kept pace with the growing number of pupils.
A generation returning to classrooms
For 12-year-old Fatima Mahmud Umar, a student at the Junior Secondary School One in Maiduguri, education offers an opportunity to pursue ambitions that years of violence have threatened for children across Borno.
Wearing a blue and white chequered hijab and her school uniform, Fatima spoke to Al Jazeera about her hopes for the future.
She expressed gratitude to her parents for supporting her education and said she hopes to become a good ambassador for her community.
Fatima also welcomed government investment in schools, including efforts to support both Islamic and Western education.
But many children across Borno have yet to regain access to regular schooling.
Violence, displacement and poverty continue to create obstacles, particularly for families struggling to rebuild their lives after years of upheaval.
Even where schools have reopened, children who missed months or years of lessons may struggle to catch up with their peers while teachers must accommodate pupils with widely different levels of preparation.
For returning students, enrolment is only the first step. Their prospects also depend on whether schools can provide the support needed to help them progress.
Rural communities left behind
The challenge is particularly pressing in rural communities, where distance, violence and limited resources can make regular schooling difficult.
In the Gubio Local Government Area, residents have raised concerns about children who remain outside formal education despite the government’s reconstruction efforts.
Bukar Abdullahi, 49, highlighted the need to enrol more children during a town hall meeting in Gubio.
While commending the state government for investing in education, Abdullahi drew attention to the difficulties facing rural communities.
For families living far from functioning schools, distance can remain an obstacle. Financial pressures and concerns about safety may also affect decisions about whether children attend.
Although the government’s figures suggest improved access, they do not show how evenly progress is distributed between urban centres and rural communities.
Addressing those disparities will require more than classrooms. Schools also need qualified teachers, learning materials and measures to help families keep their children enrolled.
Expanding Islamic education
Alongside conventional schools, Borno authorities are seeking to widen educational opportunities through Arabic and Islamic institutions.
Through the Borno State Arabic and Sangaya Education Board, the government is working to integrate aspects of traditional Islamic learning into a system offering recognised qualifications and pathways to further study.
The establishment of Higher Islamic Colleges is part of that effort.
“This intervention reflects our commitment to building an inclusive education system that integrates spiritual development with academic and vocational advancement,” Zulum said.

items.text:
Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
- Published
Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.
It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.
Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.
"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.
After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.
But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.
When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.
"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."
Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.
She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.
Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.
It is the first time police have broken down murders by gender, so it is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years.
There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.
South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.
Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa
The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confront widespread violence against women
In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.
But in places like Kokstad and Kempton Park, both in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.
For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.
Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.
"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."
He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.
The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.
The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.
According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.
This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".
Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.
Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.
"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."
Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.
Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".
Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.
Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.
In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.
Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.
Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.
The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.
Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.
Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.
"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."
Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.
Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempto

Drone attack on Colombia police base injures civilians, including infant
Far-right President De la Espriella steps up offensive as rebel groups strike back with drone strikes, roadside bombs.
A drone attack on a police base in the Colombian city of Cucuta has injured at least three civilians, including an infant, and damaged 60 homes.
Officials did not immediately say who was responsible for the attack on Monday that struck the base belonging to the Norte de Santander police.
Orlando Roa, who lives near the base, told local media that his 18-month-old grandson was among those injured and was being treated at a nearby hospital.
The attack came as far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella steps up an offensive against rebel groups and drug gangs that has resulted in the military capturing several mid-level commanders.
Armed groups have responded by attacking military bases and police stations with small drones, rockets made with gas canisters and roadside bombs. De la Espriella, who took office in August, has cancelled peace negotiations with rebel groups that were under way under his predecessor, leftist Gustavo Petro.
Cucuta, a city near Colombia’s border with Venezuela, is a major trade hub and a centre for criminal groups profiting from the drug trade and other kinds of smuggling. Rebel groups, including the National Liberation Army and the FARC-EMC, also operate in the nearby Catatumbo region.
In 2016, a peace deal between the Colombian government and the FARC led to the demobilisation of more than 14,000 fighters.
However, some border areas in Colombia have seen a surge of violence as smaller armed groups try to seize territory abandoned by the FARC, where the government has been slow to provide security and basic services.
Another police station in the Cesar region was also attacked with drones on Monday, injuring a police officer. On Saturday, one soldier was killed, and 12 others were injured during an attack with drones and rockets on a military base also in Cesar.
Both incidents remain under investigation, according to local officials.

After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.
Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.
Konstantinos Tzolakis (Hull City): If you watched the Brighton game and wondered how on earth Hull won it was because Konstantinos Tzolakis was in goal. An unbelievable performance with five or six top-class saves. Big moments, big personality, he has stepped up every time. He's been one of the players of the season - I know it's a bit too early to crown people but if it stopped now he has to be goalkeeper of the season.
James Hill (Bournemouth): He backed up getting into the England squad. Sometimes when people get called up they start to get above their stations but he didn't do that at all. He was in a really good state of form. A cheeky assist as well but defensively solid. He has been in my team a few times now - a centre-half who does his job without complaining.
Malick Thiaw (Newcastle): He divides opinion but he played really well and got his goal.
Keane Lewis-Potter (Brentford): Two goals against Everton and that was before the sending-off of James Tarkowski. Performed well again. Sneaky bargain buy of the century to be honest.
Noah Okafor (Leeds): Two goals again. Leeds battered Chelsea and made them look unbelievably average. Nobody has been talking about how sneaky good Leeds have been, some really big performances this season.
Jack Rudoni (Coventry): Two assists in a must-win game against Crystal Palace. He stepped up big, fair play to him.
Elliott Anderson (Manchester City): The only person who actually showed a pulse in this game. He got a goal and showed pace and showed he wanted to be there. He tried his best to win a game of football.
Luca Williams-Barnett (Tottenham): Young man, a with goal and an assist. He just gave Spurs a spark we haven't seen for probably six or seven years now. He gave them that spark instantly and fair play to De Zerbi for putting him in. All the money spent, who knew it would be a home-grown talent in their youth team who would step up and really get the Spurs fans excited.
Florian Wirtz (Liverpool): Unbelievable performance. He has had a bit of a purple patch since Jurgen Klopp has taken over Germany. Did really well in terms of finding the gaps, drifting between players and finding through balls and now adding goals. Now we are seeing the player we saw in Germany and I am buzzing for him.
Oli McBurnie (Hull City): The man of the moment. He works really hard, he does everything for the team to make sure they are there. He is solid defensively but then he gets two shots and two goals. Top performance from him.
Rio Ngumoha (Liverpool): He made Diogo Dalot look like he'd never played a game before, not the fact he has played over 250 games for Manchester United and has gone to World Cups with Portugal and made him look childish, Ran him every time and twisted him inside out and got his goal.
Frank Lampard (Coventry): In the biggest game of the season so far for him he made sure he got the job done. Big win. No new-manager bounce for Palace as Lampard gets the job done and he made some big calls.

items.title: EU plans sports ban in sweeping new Russia sanctions proposal
items.summary:
EU plans sports ban in sweeping new Russia sanctions proposal
Proposed sanctions aim to curb Russian crypto financing and ‘propaganda’ in sports.
The European Commission has proposed new sanctions against Russia targeting its banks, crypto platforms, and participation in sporting events.
Commission
items.text:
EU plans sports ban in sweeping new Russia sanctions proposal
Proposed sanctions aim to curb Russian crypto financing and ‘propaganda’ in sports.
The European Commission has proposed new sanctions against Russia targeting its banks, crypto platforms, and participation in sporting events.
Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen introduced the 22nd package of sanctions on Monday, which includes a ban on Russian teams and individual athletes competing under the country’s flag at events in the European Union.
“We are striking harder at Russia’s ways to finance its war, by targeting its banks and crypto platforms,” von der Leyen wrote in a post on X, adding that the EU will be “shutting the door to its participation in European sports and cultural events”.
Economic pressure
Von der Leyen said 60 banks will be removed from the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) messaging system used for international payments under the new proposals, which are intended to maintain economic pressure on Russia, almost five years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
She announced the creation of a crypto sanctions task force seeking to curb countries helping Russia to evade sanctions.
The commission also proposed a ban on visas for Russians who had fought in the war in Ukraine.
“Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries,” von der Leyen said.
‘Propaganda activities’
The plan also put forward restrictions on financial flows from Russian sponsors to sports and cultural associations based in the EU. Russian nationals would also no longer be allowed to hold leadership positions on the governing bodies of sports federations.
“Sports events cannot be a forum for propaganda activities,” said von der Leyen.
The proposed package must be endorsed by all 27 EU member countries before going into force and comes just over a month after the bloc posted the largest listing of sanctions against Russia, targeting about 1,600 Russian officials and companies linked to its arms industry.
The EU has already slapped sanctions on more than 4,200 people and entities, including Russian President Vladimir Putin and several energy companies.

items.title: 14 countries acknowledge ICJ ruling of genocide against Rohingya
items.summary:
14 countries acknowledge ICJ ruling of genocide against Rohingya
14 from Europe, Africa and Oceania have acknowledged a landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, calling on the country to comply with its obligations under int
items.text:
14 countries acknowledge ICJ ruling of genocide against Rohingya
14 from Europe, Africa and Oceania have acknowledged a landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, calling on the country to comply with its obligations under international law. The United Kingdom separately announced sanctions against five senior Myanmar military figures and said it would formally recognise the genocide.
The UK and 13 other countries on Monday "acknowledged" the top UN court's ruling that Myanmar perpetrated genocide against its Rohingya minority as London announced new sanctions.
The foreign ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, The Gambia and the United Kingdom said Myanmar had "violated its obligations under the Genocide Convention".
"We underscore that the Court's judgment is binding upon Myanmar and call on Myanmar to comply fully with its obligations under international law, including the Court's decision," they said in a joint statement.
The UK separately said it "formally recognises" genocide against the Rohingya and announced sanctions on five senior military figures.
"The horrific violence and persecution inflicted on the Rohingya cannot go unanswered," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said.
The sanctions include asset freezes and travel bans, a Foreign Office statement said, adding that London "also intends to introduce legislation targeting the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar".
"The UK is providing an additional £5m in new funding to support Rohingya and other communities with essential lifesaving and life-affirming services to approximately 350,000 people who need it most in Rakhine state, where humanitarian need is most acute," the statement added.
It said a further £3 million would "go towards strengthening accountability and justice for survivors of human rights abuses across Myanmar."
On November 19 in a historic verdict, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 crackdown in the western Rakhine state.
The ruling was the first time in the ICJ's 80-year history that it has determined that a state committed genocide.
Myanmar's government called the ruling unfair and a "great disappointment".
Shortly after the verdict, Britain announced it would expel Myanmar's defence attache.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Trump claims credit for Huang’s return, raising concerns over federal government meddling in corporate board decisions.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s dramatic return to the helm of the world’s most valuable chipmaker, less tha
items.text:
What Nvidia’s Jensen Huang’s return means for Washington and Wall Street?
Trump claims credit for Huang’s return, raising concerns over federal government meddling in corporate board decisions.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s dramatic return to the helm of the world’s most valuable chipmaker, less than two weeks after his resignation, has sent the company’s stock soaring.
At the same time, the White House’s involvement in his reinstatement has raised questions about Silicon Valley’s growing sway in Washington, with United States President Donald Trump claiming to have been a linchpin in the decision.
What happened?
The saga began less than two weeks ago when Huang resigned amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Beijing has denied that Alice Huang is a spy. She previously led Megaspeed, a company that had a business relationship with Nvidia, the Santa Clara, California-based tech giant.
Nvidia’s board had begun an investigation into the allegations, but Huang resigned before it reached a conclusion.
In his absence, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress took over as interim chief executive while the board searched for a permanent successor.
However, Huang’s departure quickly prompted a backlash from influential figures in Silicon Valley. A petition calling for his reinstatement attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including that of SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
Analysts also warned that losing Huang could significantly undermine Nvidia’s market value. Dan Ives, managing partner at Yorkville Ives, estimated that Huang’s departure could wipe as much as 30 percent off the company’s valuation.
By Monday, Nvidia brought Huang back to lead the company.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C Jones, chair of the board, in a news statement. That was an about-face from just a few days ago when the board ruled out bringing back Huang.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang added.
How has the Trump administration been involved?
Trump said on Monday that he played a central role in Huang’s reinstatement, saying in social media posts and in an interview with CNBC that his intervention had been instrumental in the board’s decision.
Trump said he had participated in the board meeting, following efforts by influential Silicon Valley figures to persuade the president to intervene in the leadership crisis, which analysts say lacked a clear succession plan.
Trump told CNBC that the stock market reaction to Huang’s resignation from Nvidia “probably” factored into his decision to push for the CEO’s reinstatement, although his view of the long-term benefit of having Huang at the helm of the company was the bigger weight, the Reuters news agency reported.
“I think this move is unprecedented in the sense that a sitting president has exerted very public pressure on a corporate board to make a particular decision,” Aleksandar Tomic, associate dean for strategy, innovation and technology at Boston College, told Al Jazeera.
Corporate governance experts say greater transparency is needed about the extent of Trump’s involvement in Nvidia’s leadership decisions.
“A board can take input from [the] government; what it should not do is let any outside party choose the CEO without explaining to shareholders why,” Martin Mulyadi, professor of accounting at Shenandoah University’s College of Business, Engineering & Technology, told Al Jazeera.
The intervention comes amid divisions within the Trump administration over Nvidia’s business practices and its relationship with China.
The Department of Justice (DOJ) and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) continue to investigate the company, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has emerged as one of its most vocal critics.
Bessent has questioned whether Nvidia facilitated chip sales to China to bolster its financial performance, alleging in an interview with Fox News that the AI chip giant had engaged in “seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings”.
He has also called for Nvidia to appoint a new chief executive from outside the company.
Meanwhile, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faces allegations that he delayed restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China, raising questions about whether his decisions were influenced by the financial interests of his former firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, which is now controlled by his two sons.
Democratic lawmakers are seeking to determine whether the firm’s holdings or business relationships benefitted from the Commerce Department’s failure to impose those restrictions.
“The key issue is how much of Nvidia’s revenue may be coming from sales that would not pass increased scrutiny vis-a-vis export control violations. Given accusations within the government of lax monitoring and enforcement, it is also not clear that Nvidia had robust controls, and their inability to stick to the CEO decision makes it doubtful that they will be able to implement it in the future,” Tomic said.
What precedent does the decision set?
Trump’s involvement has also raised broader questions about the relationship between the federal government and corporate America, particularly the extent to which a president should influence decisions traditionally reserved for a company’s board of directors.
Tomic says that the level of direct pressure Trump placed on Nvidia’s board, including his participation in discussions about Huang’s reinstatement, is highly unusual for a sitting president.
The precedent could ultimately backfire on Republicans, Tomic warned, particularly as Democrats prepare to take control of both the House and Senate in January. Democrats have historically pushed for greater oversight of large corporations, and the incom

items.title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
items.summary:
US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
- Published
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The US Department of Commerce announced on Monday that it planned to add
items.text:
US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
- Published
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The US Department of Commerce announced on Monday that it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks, a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funneling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the Commerce announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month, when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had carried on an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang was thought by the US intelligence apparatus to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
Days later, another alleged affair surfaced involving Jensen Huang and the CEO resigned. On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The Commerce Department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years prior to the affair incident.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China. China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China, Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, is its largest customer.

items.title: Tarkowski's first Premier League red ruins Moyes' night - was it deserved?
items.summary:
Tarkowski's first Premier League red ruins Moyes' night - was it deserved?
- Published
It had been some run for Everton captain James Tarkowski.
Prior to Monday night, the defender had received 74 yellow cards in the Premier League but had never been sent off - a top-flight record.
But that run came
items.text:
Tarkowski's first Premier League red ruins Moyes' night - was it deserved?
- Published
It had been some run for Everton captain James Tarkowski.
Prior to Monday night, the defender had received 74 yellow cards in the Premier League but had never been sent off - a top-flight record.
But that run came to an end at Brentford as he was given his first red card in his 351st Premier League appearance, although the decision has attracted plenty of debate.
His dismissal crucially means he will miss Sunday's Merseyside derby and also ruined David Moyes' record-breaking night as he took charge of his 593rd game as Everton boss - more than anyone else in the club's history.
The 4-0 loss was also the heaviest defeat Everton have had since Moyes returned to the club at the start of last year.
Tarkowski's dismissal proved a big talking point during and after the match, with opinions split on whether he should have gone. Even Moyes wasn't sure.
He told BBC Match of the Day: "My thoughts at the time, I didn't think it was but when I've looked at it again I think his foot high. Is there enough force for it to be a red card? Not sure about that."
Why did Tarkowski get sent off?
So what exactly happened?
Just 15 minutes after Keane Lewis-Potter scored his second deflected strike of the evening, Everton skipper Tarkowski thundered into a challenge on Brentford's Yehor Yarmoliuk.
He won the ball but also followed through with the challenge forcefully. Initially, referee Craig Pawson deemed a foul and a yellow card was enough.
But, after an intervention from the video assistant referee (VAR) and studying the replay, Pawson changed the yellow for a red.
The Premier League match centre said on X: "After VAR review, the referee overturned the original decision of yellow card for Tarkowski for the challenge on Yarmoliuk and issued a red card for serious foul play.
"VAR: 'Point of contact is on the shin. He's got speed and intensity. Studs are high.'
"REF: 'After review, Everton No.6 commits a challenge that endangers his opponent's safety, making contact with the studs onto the shin. Cancelling the yellow card - and a red card.'"
'Game's gone' or '100% red'? Experts are split
Referees are asked to take into account several considerations for what counts as serious foul play including the speed of the challenge, its intensity, force and what degree of control there was.
But, as always, there was plenty of debate about whether it was the correct decision.
BBC Sport's football issues correspondent Dale Johnson, said: "Really not sure about this as a VAR red card.
"Yes, Tarkowski absolutely ticks the boxes for speed and intensity and leading high with studs showing.
"But the question marks are that Tarkowski made only small contact and didn't have a straight leg when he did so.
"Maybe his reputation played a part? Remember, he wrongly escaped a VAR red card against Liverpool for a challenge, which was along the same lines. He won the ball and then followed through into Alexis Mac Allister. Thought that was a far stronger challenge."
BBC Radio 5 Live's - and former Blackburn Rovers striker - Chris Sutton, said on X: "Come on that's not a red… the game's gone."
Former Arsenal striker Alan Smith agreed the decision was harsh. He told Sky Sports: "Ten years ago we wouldn't have looked at it once and now we still [frame] it on the follow-through. I just can't see it.
"Only Tarkowski knows if he wanted to leave it high or if it was natural. The follow-through was just natural momentum.
"There's a bit of anger in there from Tarkowski and it's a little high but only he knows if he wanted to leave a little more on Yarmoliuk there."
Opinion was far from unanimous though, with both pundits in the Sky Sports studio adamant it was a clear red.
Former Liverpool centre-back Jamie Carragher said: "It's a red card. Tarkowski has got previous for tackles like that. He is a 90s defender, he tackles like that.
"He follows through with such force, it is excessive. You want to give him the benefit of the doubt but it's a red card."
He added: "You could argue was it a big enough mistake for VAR to get involved but I think we are splitting hairs. He doesn't need to do this."
While ex-Totenham defender Toby Alderweireld added: "It's a red card, he knows what he is doing. 100%."
'Never a red' or a 'clear' sending off - what you thought
Josh, Sheffield: Never a red for Tarkowski and I'm a Liverpool fan. What's he meant to do? Stop momentum. It's a good tackle and the player runs into the natural follow through
Robin, Essex: Another game ruined by VAR! Not straight leg tackle you can surely see he turned his foot around. Poor!
Rob, Manchester: These sorts of VAR decisions are making me turn off football. Why pay all that money to watch arbitrary decisions impact the game?
Lee: It is a sad day when a good tackle gets a player sent off. You slow anything down and dissect it you can find wrongs. Yellow was a bit much and the red ridiculous, we need ex players in the VAR decisions too.
Max, Oldham: What a load of nonsense the red card is. Tarkowski can't stop his momentum. VAR has ruined another game, plus what is the ref doing? He had a chance to stick with the yellow card. Another case of an official who has never played the game.
Paul, St Asaph: Tarkowski has got away with that same foul a few times. Do think he's the type of player to leave one in on purpose.
Anon: Yes it's a red - Tarkowski knows what he's doing, it's frustration and wanting to leave a bit on the player.
Chris, Chelmsford: He does it all the time at the borderline but about time he got one.
Woody, London: Lack of refinement masked as passion, classic Tarkowski tackle there… glad to see him off.
George, Birmingham: Studs up in a tackle, he has to go. A clear red card for me.

items.title: Butt of the joke: Trump impersonator mocks president at Canada press dinner
items.summary:
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a Donald Trump impersonator who mocked the US president to raucous laughter from a crowd of politicians and journalists at a parliamentary press gallery dinner on Saturday.
With coiffed hair and an ill-fitting suit, comedian Mark
items.text:
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a Donald Trump impersonator who mocked the US president to raucous laughter from a crowd of politicians and journalists at a parliamentary press gallery dinner on Saturday.
With coiffed hair and an ill-fitting suit, comedian Mark Critch – who portrays the president on the sketch show This Hour Has 22 Minutes – danced on to the stage and lampooned the trade war Trump started as well as the president’s threats to annex Canada.
“We’re going to have a great deal,” Critch said, channeling Trump’s distinct mannerisms. “There’s only one thing standing in the way: me, because I’m crazy.”
The fake Trump continued that he was “so popular we just had a big, blue wave”, a reference to the Democratic rout of Republicans in this month’s US midterm elections.
He also mocked Trump’s frequent mentions of other men’s physiques, saying of the comedian Mark McKinney, who was portraying Carney, that he had “a great ass – doesn’t he? What a beautiful ass, he’s got such an incredible ass.”
He earned the most laughter of his short appearance for saying of Carney: “I don’t call him the governor to his face, because I’m a coward”. The real Trump has frequently attempted to insult Canada’s leaders by calling them governor, not prime minister, suggesting Canada is a US state.
The annual dinner, attended by media, political leaders and lobbyists, is often defined by carefully written jokes by the staff of party leaders.
Throughout his own 16-minute set, Carney poked fun at his political rivals, the media and the US president.
At one point, he remarked: “Damn, this is a tough room, and I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator.”
Clips of the dinner, including the crowd laughing at the president, have circulated widely on US media.
The newly appointed governor general, Louise Arbour, also gave a speech, including a nod to the prime minister’s decision to travel extensively around the globe.
“Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be,” she said.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, also used the evening to poke fun at his own reputation.
“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable prick to journalists,” he said. “And when I hear things like that, I say once again, he’s stealing all my ideas.”
He attracted a stunned silence, however, for alluding to Justin Trudeau’s relationship with Katy Perry, saying, “Trudeau is running around the world doing to a faded pop princess what he did to Canada” while prime minister, a remark that was widely criticised as demeaning to the pop star.
The New Democratic party leader, Avi Lewis, who has not yet won a seat in parliament, took a shot at Carney’s early exit from the event, as well his own party’s dismal standings. “I do not have a seat in the House of Commons, but when I am given one at dinner, I stay there all night long,” he said.

items.text:
US adds Megaspeed, at center of Nvidia scandal, to a trade blacklist
November 23, 2026
The Trump administration added Megaspeed International, the firm at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, to a trade blacklist on Monday.
That means that the Singapore-based firm will not be able to obtain US technology, including semiconductors, without obtaining a license from the US government.
The news was reported by Semafor, an American news website.
US Commerce Department under scrutiny over Nvidia scandal: What to know
The US Commerce Department had been investigating whether Megaspeed was smuggling Nvidia chips into China for more than a year, according to the Financial Times.
But tensions at the Commerce Department broke into the spotlight after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with an executive at the Singapore-based firm earlier this month.
Politicians criticized Commerce Department Secretary Howard Lutnick for not having previously added Megaspeed to the department's so-called "Entity List" despite US intelligence warnings that the company was a possible front for smuggling sensitive AI chip technology to China.
Huang briefly lost his job over the scandal as US officials said the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO on Monday, in a stunning reversal after his resignation just two weeks ago.
The New York Times reported last month that US authorities had concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with Jensen Huang.
Beijing has denied those claims and called the spy accusations "groundless."
Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
Nvidia shares soared more than 30% after the company announced it reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
Some people were happy to see him back as president of Nvidia, as videos posted to social media show.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is on track to be the next speaker of the House, called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible, and incomprehensible" and vowed Congress would reinvestigate any wrongdoing by the company and the Commerce Department.

items.summary:
California Democrat Rep. Gomez resigns following ethics report on sexual misconduct allegations
Rep. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif) says he is resigning from Congress after a bipartisan investigation released Monday found "substantial evidence" he engaged in sexual misconduct toward a House staffer.
The Hous
items.text:
California Democrat Rep. Gomez resigns following ethics report on sexual misconduct allegations
Rep. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif) says he is resigning from Congress after a bipartisan investigation released Monday found "substantial evidence" he engaged in sexual misconduct toward a House staffer.
The House Ethics Committee concluded Gomez violated House rules by "making unwelcome sexual advances and engaging in unwelcome sexual conduct towards a House staffer and disregarding the power imbalance inherent in his relationship with House staffers."
The report also says the behavior could constitute criminal sexual assault.
Gomez has served in Congress since 2017 representing parts of Los Angeles. He lost reelection this fall to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres. California uses a system where the top two vote-getters no matter the party advance to the general election. Gomez says his resignation will be effective Dec. 1.
Lisa Banks and Sarah Nesbitt, attorneys for the unnamed House staffer, wrote in a statement that their client testified to the committee truthfully and at personal risk.
"She sacrificed her own sense of safety and privacy to help reveal the ongoing misogyny and debauchery that permeates Capitol Hill," Banks and Nesbitt wrote. "Representative Gomez seems to believe that the power he wields, both as a man and as a member of Congress, makes him untouchable. Today's findings are a meaningful step toward dismantling that belief."
In a statement announcing his plan to resign, Gomez wrote that he cooperated with the investigation, but has strong disagreements with the report and its conclusions.
"Among other significant deficiencies and omissions, the report does not include key portions of my testimony that are essential to a full and fair understanding of what occurred," he wrote.
"I also have serious concerns about the process. In my interview, I answered the Committee's questions only to see my statements selectively quoted, disparaged, and disregarded throughout the final report, to which I was given no opportunity to respond."
The House Ethics Committee, which includes five Democrats and five Republicans, opened its investigation into Gomez in August following a press report of Gomez kissing a staffer from another Congressional office at a party. Gomez denied those allegations.
The committee asked Gomez to disclose whether he "ever engaged in a romantic or sexual relationship or made sexual contact with a congressional staffer." Gomez disclosed interactions with two women — telling the committee the encounters were all consensual. Both women spoke to the committee.
One denied "she had ever had a nonconsensual sexual encounter" with Gomez. The other, described as Witness 1 in the report, said she had more than one encounter with Gomez and she did not consider them consensual.
She told investigators that Gomez made sexual contact without her consent at a bar in February 2024 and then was forceful with her and tried to kiss her at his congressional office in July 2024.
Gomez denied the interactions were nonconsensual. The staffer, described as Witness 1 in the committee report, eventually left her job on Capitol Hill.
"Here, the House lost Witness 1 as a competent and able staffer because of Representative Gomez's misconduct and because of a broader culture of disrespect and toxic sexual behavior toward staff that permeates life on the Hill and is long overdue for correction," the committee wrote.
The report comes amid a broader conversation about how Congress deals with the behavior of its members, especially when it comes to sexual misconduct.
In April, Democrat Eric Swalwell of California resigned his House seat amid allegations of sexual assault and misconduct. He also denied the allegations. Rep. Tony Gonzales (R-Tex.) also resigned from the House after admitting to an affair with a former staff member.
Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) dropped his reelection bid earlier this year after the House Ethics Committee recommended he face a censure vote for allegedly harassing two young female staffers. Edwards denied the allegations.
Republican Reps. Max Miller of Ohio and Cory Mills of Florida also face House Ethics investigations stemming from allegations of domestic violence. Both deny wrongdoing.
Miller lost his reelection bid this fall and Mills lost his GOP primary.
Last week, the House Ethics Committee adopted new rules with the aim of speeding up investigations into sexual misconduct and improving transparency.

The top-25 finishers and ties at the 2026 LPGA Q-Series final qualifying stage have been awarded LPGA Tour status for 2027; Megha Ganne won the event outright, while Megan Khang - part of Team USA for the past five Solheim Cups - is one of 27 players to claim a tour card for next season
Monday 23 November 2026 23:16, UK
Megha Ganne won the 2026 LPGA Q-Series final qualifying stage as 27 tour cards were claimed for the 2027 season, with five-time USA Solheim Cup team member Megan Khang among those successful.
Khang - part of Team USA for the past five Solheim Cups - is returning to the LPGA Tour, on which she's made 259 starts since 2016, winning the 2023 CPKC Women's Open.
The top-25 finishers and ties at the conclusion of the 2026 LPGA Q-Series final qualifying were awarded LPGA Tour status for next year.
American Ganne won the final stage outright on 23 under, one shot clear of Shannon Tan and Julia Gregg in a tie for second. Min Sun7 Kim was fourth on 21 under and Xiaowen Yin one further back in fifth.
Ganne, the 2025 US Amateur champion, had actually already secured her 2027 LPGA Tour status by entering the week by finishing 11-15 on the Epson Tour.
Gregg, who finished in a share of second, has never previously had a start on the LPGA Tour.
"It feels unreal," the 25-year-old American said after clinching her place. "It's been my dream since I was four years old to play on the LPGA and now that I finally did it."

items.text:
After Nvidia’s board accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO, following reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, President Donald Trump, too, appeared to submit to the new reality. Appearing on Stephen A. Smith’s radio show shortly after the news came out, Trump said that Huang would “end up on his feet.”
Trump engineered a risky comeback for Jensen Huang
Trump got his wish to reinstate Jensen Huang at the helm of Nvidia — but investigations are still looming.
Trump engineered a risky comeback for Jensen Huang
Trump got his wish to reinstate Jensen Huang at the helm of Nvidia — but investigations are still looming.
“You know the expression, anybody can be replaced,” Trump said, floating Apple’s ex-CEO Tim Cook as a potential CEO candidate.
It didn’t take long for Trump to begin softening his approach, making it clear he’d welcome Huang back into the role of CEO even if Nvidia’s own board wasn’t ready to do so. Behind the scenes, the Trump administration was working to grease the landing for Huang’s return. And soon, Nvidia’s board changed its tune: Barely a week after insisting they all agreed to shut the door on Huang’s return, they voted unanimously to reinstate him as CEO, president, and board director.
“There’s nothing wrong with a comeback,” Trump said in a celebratory call to CNBC.
Trump then posted an image on Truth Social of Huang transposed onto Trump’s own body in the infamous photo of him raising his fist after being shot at a campaign rally. In his raised fist, Huang-on-Trump’s-body is clutching a scarlet bra, holding it high in the air.
“There’s nothing wrong with a comeback”
Even after a decisive blow to the president’s power as Democrats swept the midterm elections, Trump appears to maintain his position as a corporate kingmaker. Trump said he spoke with Huang the night prior to his reinstatement and had been in communication with the board both “directly and indirectly.” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement that “President Trump was totally involved” in the board’s decision — Trump decided near the end of last week that he wanted to lead efforts to get Huang reappointed, per The New York Times, so he asked Vice President JD Vance to act as a liaison between Huang and Nvidia’s board, providing reassurances that the move wouldn’t pose a security risk. Trump also reportedly dialed into Nvidia’s Sunday night board meeting to make the case for his return. “I made the deal,” he told CNBC on Monday.
News of Huang’s reappointment, nearly as dramatic as Sam Altman’s return to his CEO role after being voted out by OpenAI’s board in 2023, was a widespread shock to experts, analysts, and investors, particularly after Nvidia’s board had assured stakeholders on its quarterly earnings call last Tuesday that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On Monday morning, a surge in NASDAQ-100 futures hit a circuit-breaker limit and caused a halt in trading over the volatility.
Trump has meddled in other messy incidents, including by repeatedly — and perhaps illegally — extending the deadline for TikTok to complete its sale to a US entity, and, he admitted on Monday, protecting Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Although he said on CNBC that Musk is “80 percent super genius, 20 percent he has other problems,” Trump said it’s important to protect people like him and Huang. “We have to protect our brilliant people because we don’t have enough.”
But the upcoming Democratic-majority Congress could test both Huang and Trump’s influence. As Republicans prepare for an open presidential primary in 2028, at least one potential candidate appears to be breaking with the president in their skepticism of Huang and Nvidia. And Democrats seem eager to probe both Nvidia and the Trump administration.
The past couple of weeks have been tumultuous for Nvidia. Huang admitted he had had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom some US intelligence officers reportedly believed to be a potential Chinese spy. There were nearly immediate reports of an additional affair with a direct report, as well as an alleged third affair with a second employee. Megaspeed has reportedly also been investigated for a broader attempt to illegally funnel advanced Nvidia chips to China. Huang himself has pushed to open up more chip sales to China, and he reportedly lied to the Nvidia board about his infidelity. He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st.
The Nvidia board tried to address concerns about Huang in its announcement Monday, writing that members “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” It made assurances that the independent investigation it had kicked off about Huang and foreign intelligence would “proceed to conclusion” with Huang’s cooperation.
The board also said it had recently formed an entirely new National Security and Export Control Committee “comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” which is working with legal counsel and advisers who have national security experience. Nvidia will be hiring for a new C-suite position, the board said: chief compliance officer. The executive will “oversee compliance” across the company and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance committees. “NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries,” the board added.
Still, the reaction to Huang’s return reflects how small the chance of Huang’s return seemed before Trump’s efforts. items.text:
After the leather-jacketed CEO, president, and co-founder of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, his company initially announced an investigation. However, after The New York Times reported there was evidence of another affair, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported directly to him, a board meeting that night ended with Huang’s resignation, and Nvidia CFO Colette Kress was installed as the new interim CEO.
And then… Huang was back.
In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies. Saying it received input “from senior levels of the United States government,” Nvidia’s board announced his return as CEO on November 23rd, less than two weeks after his resignation.
Follow along below for all of the latest updates.
- Trump engineered a risky comeback for Jensen Huang After Nvidia’s board accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO, following reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, President Donald Trump, too, appeared to submit to the new reality. Appearing on Stephen A. Smith’s radio show shortly after the news came out, Trump said that Huang would “end up on his feet.” “You know the expression, anybody can be replaced,” Trump said, floating Apple’s ex-CEO Tim Cook as a potential CEO candidate. Read Article >
- Welcome to elite impunity, Jensen Huang I suppose I must issue a hearty congratulations to Jensen Huang. Huang is CEO of Nvidia again, to the surprise of basically everyone except President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who made sure it happened. Now, those of us who had some kind of basic education on what a “free market” is might find it objectionable to have the American president strong-arming a major American company. But our billionaire tech overlords care about the “free market” exactly as much as they care about “free speech,” which is to say not at all. Watching Silicon Valley cheer for what is, effectively, a sign of a command economy has certainly been bracing. But then, why would they give a shit? Their only real beliefs are that they should remain rich and above the law. Jensen may not have exchanged emails with Jeffrey Epstein, but he’s squarely at the Epstein table now. Read Article >
- Here’s Trump discussing the Jensen Huang situation on TV for 10 minutes. Trump did the TV circuit this morning to talk up how involved he was in Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO on Monday. He said on CNBC that he spoke to Nvidia’s board, adding, “I convinced them.”
- Jensen Huang says he’ll be a ‘better CEO’ as staff applauds his return Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia’s office as CEO today to a crowd of applauding employees who stood and filmed the cofounder’s first moments back. “Thank you all for the second chances. I’m gonna be a better CEO the second time around,” Huang said, as shown in a video of his return. Read Article >
- How Jensen Huang ended up as Nvidia CEO again The Jensen Huang era of Nvidia nearly came to an end this month. Huang, who three decades ago cofounded what’s come to be considered one of the most important companies in AI, resigned from his role on November 12th over mounting scrutiny around his alleged affairs. Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and that he “created problems for the board.” Huang’s resignation came after weeks of escalating problems, both personal and professional. First, reporting from The New York Times said he had a “close relationship” with a woman passing intelligence to China. Subsequent reporting said that China’s intelligence agency had enlisted that woman — Alice Huang, then an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed — to spy on Nvidia’s leader, and that the Singapore-based company was under investigation for potentially smuggling AI chips to China. Stories followed that indicated Huang was having an affair with Alice as well as an Nvidia executive, vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell. Read Article >
- Jensen Huang has already come back to Nvidia’s offices. Employees applauded for his return.

Trump said he “believed very strongly” that Huang should be reinstated. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation, and the investigation showed that he did — I mean, he had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents. But he did nothing wrong.” Read Article >

You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates, and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees, a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable company.
