What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
- Published
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.
Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.
Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".
Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".
And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.
Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?
The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.
Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.
This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.
Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.
He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.
Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.
"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.
The wider political backdrop was still more revealing.
The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.
And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.
The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.
A majority that may yet offer hope
Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.
Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.
Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action.
So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them?
The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels.
Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received.
"This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared.
Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU."
Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies.
The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance.
So is it possible for a majority of countries to outvote those blocking progress?
The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, has acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible. Others want countries prepared to move faster to make their own agreements outside the formal talks.
But there is a reason the UN climate process depends on consensus. International climate co-operation is largely voluntary.
Voting might produce more ambitious agreements on paper, but would it persuade the governments that had been outvoted to act? Consensus also offers some protection to smaller and poorer nations that might otherwise find themselves overruled by the most powerful countries.
Meanwhile, the failure to agree a summit declaration does not mean climate action stops. Solar pan

items.text:
We are proud to announce something that our small team of very dedicated people at Kagi has been building for a long time – the public beta of Kagi Mail. A private email and calendar with a @kagimail.com address, or with your own domains.
If you’ve already swapped Google Search for Kagi and Chrome for Orion, your inbox is probably the last big piece of your digital life still at Google. Now you can move that too.
Try Kagi Mail free for 60 days
$99/year (+ Sales Tax) after that. Included with Kagi Ultimate.
Why we built it
Does the world need another email service? We asked ourselves that question more than once. There are great ones out there, and we’re fans of what Fastmail and Tuta are doing. We still built our own, for the same reason we build everything at Kagi: technology should do its job and then get out of your way.
For email, that job is to be fast, private, and secure. On top of that, it should help you stay on track with what’s important: bring forward what you need to act on, respond to, or acknowledge, and quietly handle the rest.
Kagi Mail also has to treat you the way Kagi Search and Orion do: no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in.
Already a Kagi member?
Kagi Mail is included in Ultimate. Sign in with your Kagi account, and you’re set. AI features draw from your existing Allowance. On another plan, or no Kagi account yet? After the free 60-day trial, you can get Kagi Mail for $99/year (+ Sales Tax).
How it works: A service and a client, on open standards
To deliver the experience we believe in, we built the full stack: hosting for your addresses and domains, plus the mail and calendar apps. It runs on open standards and open-source infrastructure (the Stalwart server, IMAP, JMAP, and CalDAV), so you can use Kagi’s apps or any compatible client you already like.
The basics
- A @kagimail.com address
- Unlimited aliases
- Unlimited domains
- Built-in Calendar
- 50 GB of storage
Intelligence
- Organize your mail in your own words. Brief it the way you’d brief an assistant: “Label anything where beta users send product feedback. It might come from @kagimail.com, but use judgment.” You decide what permissions each rule gets (read the content, or skip the inbox).
- Inbox Highlights show what needs you today, and learn from what you dismiss.
- Ask your inbox in plain language and get direct answers with the source email, including text inside scanned PDFs and photos.
- Newsletter view reads newsletters like a feed, out of the way of real mail.
- Responsible AI, with one switch to turn it all off. You control what AI is allowed to do and infer.
Private by default
- Tracking pixels and remote images are blocked or proxied, so senders can’t tell when or where you opened their mail.
- Sender screening holds new senders until you approve them, so they never reach your inbox uninvited.
- Suspicious senders trigger a phishing warning, while verified senders show their (BMI) logo.
No ads, ever. No profiling, no selling, no sharing your data.
For teams and families
- Shared addresses on your domain (team@, info@, family@): create an alias, then choose which people have access to it
- Sign in through a social login, or your organization’s own identity provider (OIDC)
- Coming soon: Shared mailboxes
Kagi integration
- Kagi Translate is built in
- Email Assistant: Write to assistant@kagimail.com for answers about your mail (actions coming soon)
- Proofread and translation included while you write emails
For power users and developers
- Keyboard-first: command palette, shortcuts, and search operators
- Rule-based filtering with Sieve, no AI involved
- MCP server with read access to your mail
- Works with Apple Mail, Thunderbird, and any IMAP/JMAP/CalDAV client, with automatic setup
What’s not here yet
We will keep adding new capabilities – here’s what to expect over the next few quarters.
Until the mobile apps arrive, use the mobile web app or any IMAP/JMAP client, such as Apple Mail or Thunderbird.
Our “no lock-in” promise to you
Leaving Kagi Mail is as easy as joining it. Your mail, calendar, and workflows are yours, and you can export them at any time, through standard protocols and a one-click export experience. You’ll keep access to your mailbox for six months after leaving Kagi Mail. You can send and receive emails for the first 60 days, then read and export your mail with one click for the remaining four months. We build an ecosystem so things work better together for those who want it, not to trap anyone.
Try Kagi Mail free for 60 days
$99/year (+ Sales Tax) after that. Included with Kagi Ultimate.
We want Kagi Mail to be the first email account we’d create for our children. We’re not there yet, but it is a high bar we hold ourselves to, and every feature in this beta is a step toward it: a calm, safe place to communicate, and a window onto an internet that treats you as a person, not a product who’s been tracked, targeted, and sold to.
We can build it this way because of you. Kagi has no ad business, and no one pushing us to monetize your inbox; you’re not a dataset for ads or AI. You are here because you believe the internet can be built differently. Thank you.

items.text:
Amazon has agreed to acquire a good chunk of Israeli startup Decart.
The e-commerce and cloud giant is paying $7.5 billion for the startup, according to Bloomberg.
Decart has made a name for itself building interactive real-time world models — most recently Oasis 3 — and AI video generation tools. But under the hood, the company stands out for its Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), software that helps AI models to run efficiently on Nvidia, Amazon, and Google’s hardware.
As part of the deal, Amazon will acquire the technology behind DOS, as well as Decart’s founding team and team of AI researchers and engineers, Amazon said in a blog post.
“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, quantum computing, at Amazon. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.”
Amazon, which has been so far been using its Trainium chips at its own data centers, is preparing to start selling them to customers as a competitor to Nvidia. Decart’s technology could make it easier for customers to run their workloads on Amazon chips, rather than Nvidia’s, which has been the gold standard so far.
Decart and Amazon did not immediately return requests for comment.

items.text:
Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
- Published
Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the charity Oxfam says, external.
Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza "will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival".
In response, the Israeli embassy in the UK said the report "falls short of professional standards".
Behar also accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza".
Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. It maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.
Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.
The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".
Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.
"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.
She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.
With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.
Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.
UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.
The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.
The Israeli embassy sharply criticised the report, arguing that it relied on satellite imagery "and unverified assumptions, and its methodology lacks the academic rigour needed to withstand serious scrutiny".
It said the report drew conclusions about Gaza's soil and groundwater without considering the excavation of hundreds of kilometres of tunnels by Hamas, rendering it fundamentally flawed.
Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.
A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.
"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."
Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.
"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."
At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.
Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

items.title: Jensen Huang isn’t out of the woods yet
items.summary:
It’s safe to say no one expected this.
Monday morning, Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia, after resigning the position following news of multiple affairs, including one with a subordinate and one with a woman tied to Chinese intelligence services. With so much of the AI industry built on top of
items.text:
It’s safe to say no one expected this.
Monday morning, Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia, after resigning the position following news of multiple affairs, including one with a subordinate and one with a woman tied to Chinese intelligence services. With so much of the AI industry built on top of Nvidia’s AI infrastructure, Huang’s departure looked like an imminent threat to the business — and the mood on his return has been ecstatic. Share prices are rocketing back up, particularly for neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, and the Nasdaq rose 7% on the news.
Still, tech leaders should be clear-eyed about all the problems likely to come with Huang’s reinstatement. President Trump is already telling reporters that the US government found no national security concerns resulting from the affair, but the broader national security concerns aren’t so easy to dismiss, and Trump’s involvement may do more harm than good for Nvidia and its partners. This isn’t the end of the problems caused by Huang’s affairs; it’s likely just the beginning.
Most importantly, serious questions remain about how Nvidia chips were smuggled into China, and how much Nvidia knew about it. Among Jensen Huang’s defenders, it’s become common to question whether Alice Huang was really a spy, but it’s clear that a lot of restricted chips were flowing into China through her company. Just this weekend, the New York Times reported sustained contact between Alice Huang and a member of China’s Ministry of State Security during the same period she was having an affair with Jensen Huang.
With Democrats in control of Congress, including investigative bodies like the House Oversight Committee, there are plenty of ways to force the issue. Nvidia’s role in violating US export controls would likely have been the subject of prolonged uncomfortable investigation, whether Huang returned or not. But with him back in the CEO’s seat, there will be a lot more riding on any revelations that come up — and any new revelations will damage Nvidia as a company alongside Huang himself.
Then there are the questions raised by the pardon itself. It’s unprecedented in American history for a sitting president to intervene to clear a CEO accused of being a national security risk. Simply pressing the Department of Justice to exonerate Huang would have been a scandal, but calling the Nvidia board goes significantly further. Huang has already donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom project, so it’s easy to make the case that Trump was intervening on behalf of a donor, setting national security risks aside for his personal benefit.
All of this is happening just as Democrats retake Congress, with all of its associated investigative powers. Even if they can’t fire Huang or remove Trump, there are lots of uncomfortable questions that are still unanswered. Was there any Department of Justice inquiry into whether Huang had committed a crime, or did Trump make the call on his own? Did the intelligence services make any official assessment that could be subpoenaed into the congressional record? Investigating Democrats will be particularly interested in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees export controls and retains significant financial ties to the industry through his firm, Cantor Fitzgerald.
If all of this sounds exhausting, you’re getting a sense of what the next year will be like for anyone following national news. Congress will keep a steady drip of embarrassing revelations, milking as much political juice as possible out of Huang and everyone associated with him. Trump will keep lashing out, often making things worse for everyone involved. (Trump’s statement to CBS, which defends Huang in racist terms while also accusing him of treason, is an early taste.) It’s going to be ugly and sad, and the most successful tech company of the last decade will be right at the center of it.
I have to assume that this was the scenario the board was concerned about when it decided to remove Huang two weeks ago. Since then, the cost of removing him has gone up: an open letter from Nvidia’s employees and partners, a tanking stock market and, ultimately, direct intervention from the President of the United States.
But nothing has lowered the cost of keeping Huang, and the ugly scenario the board foresaw earlier this month is still very much in place. We’re about to see it come to life.

items.title: Barbados town’s three-year deal with Bristol ‘part of the reparative process’
items.summary:
A town in Barbados known as “Little Bristol” has signed a “twinning’” agreement with the UK city, marking a new chapter in a centuries-long relationship rooted in the transatlantic slave trade.
Barbados says the new partnership between Speightstown and Bristol is part of its wider push for reparator
items.text:
A town in Barbados known as “Little Bristol” has signed a “twinning’” agreement with the UK city, marking a new chapter in a centuries-long relationship rooted in the transatlantic slave trade.
Barbados says the new partnership between Speightstown and Bristol is part of its wider push for reparatory justice, built in small steps rather than around a multi-trillion-pound claim.
Colin Jordan, the island’s labour minister, signed a three-year memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Bristol city council leader, Tony Dyer, at City Hall on Friday.
Speightstown is the second-largest town in Barbados. In the 17th and 18th centuries its port shipped sugar, produced by enslaved African people, to Bristol. A bar bearing the name is still a popular venue within the island, Jordan said.
In an interview after the ceremony, Jordan said the agreement sat firmly within the island nation’s wider push for reparations, led by the prime minister, Mia Mottley.
“I see the MOU as part of the reparative process,” he said. “It is doing it in a complementary way because it is focused on the relationships between two towns, two cities, two peoples.”
He was careful with his language. “People get emotive about reparations,” said the politician, who is also MP for St Peter, the parish where Speightstown sits. “The word reparations comes from the word repair.”
Defensiveness, he continued, had threatened progress around the conversation. “The walls go up, and then it’s difficult for the message to get through.”
The agreement has no money attached to it and Bristol city council confirmed there was no dedicated funding for major projects involved.
However, it does set out a framework for cooperation on heritage, education, tourism, culture and the creative economy. The exact terms are to be determined through a series of discussions.
Jordan said the money question was settled. “There is not going to be some grand $4tn something somewhere,” he said. “It’s going to be building block by building block.”
He offered a Barbadian proverb to make the point that steady progress was better than extravagant windfalls: “A sheep head a day is better than a cow head a year.”
The MOU recognises the relationship began in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. “Acknowledging that, we believe, is probably half of the repair,” he said.
He described a relationship that ran one way for roughly two centuries. “Bristol and the UK benefited from the extraction of wealth from Barbados and Speightstown,” he said. The aim now was one that was “mutually beneficial, inclusive”.
Jordan expected exchanges between schools and universities, and between cricket and football bodies – and also pointed to trade.
Repair, he argued, was not only financial. “Value is not just currency,” he said. He gave the example of a Speightstown schoolchild whose parents unable to afford a school bag, helped through a link with a Bristol school. He also suggested the relationship could offer “psychological repair” to Bristolians uneasy about their ancestors’ part in slavery.
‘Not a shelf document’
The MOU runs to November 2029. Jordan has said it “will not become a ‘shelf’ document” but will serve as “a roadmap, as well as our motivation”. He was already looking to 2030, the 400th anniversary of Speightstown’s founding, for a successor agreement.
Dyer said the deal was “firmly about the future” but should be honest about the past. At the ceremony, he said much of the work lay ahead and warned against signing the agreement and “putting it in the cupboard”.
“Bristol and Speightstown have a long and complex shared history, and signing this agreement is an important opportunity both to recognise that past and to decide together how we can build on our relationship.
“Our connections were shaped by the transatlantic trafficking and enslavement of African people and the sugar trade. It is important that we are open and honest about that history, while working with communities in Bristol and Barbados to deepen our understanding of it.”
Bristol is pursuing the same model elsewhere. A parallel MOU with Odesa, in Ukraine, covers the same period.
Beyond Bristol
Edmund Hinkson, Barbados’s high commissioner to the UK, who witnessed the signing, placed the deal within a longer history. Barbados’s 1650 slave code, he noted, defined Black people as chattel, and was later copied across the Caribbean and the Americas.
Hinkson said Barbados was not looking for the trillions of pounds that economists, including the Brattle Group, have estimated is owed for two centuries of unpaid labour.
“We know that the UK is not going to pay that,” he said, although he noted that British taxpayers, including Caribbean ones, serviced the debt used to compensate 46,000 enslavers in 1834, until 2015.
The high commissioner commended Bristol’s “maturity” in recognising the historical link between Barbados and the city’s role in the transatlantic trafficking of Africans into the Caribbean, including Barbados.
He said he believed that the Black Lives Matter’ protests in 2020, which included the toppling of the statue of enslaver Edward Colston, had propelled that recognition and education of Bristolians.
When asked to expand on the point afterwards, Hinkson said the Black Lives Matter movement did not drive Barbados’s reparations stance, but reiterated his belief that it had shaped the UK response. He pointed to the recent Commonwealth summit in Antigua where, he said, a British prime minister recognised the need for “structured and respectful dialogue” over a formal apology for Britain’s role in enslavement.
Speightstown also has a twinning-style MOU with Reading, formally signed in 2003, and Charleston, South Carolina, part of the Gullah Geechee corridor, in the US.
The signing with Bristol comes days before Barbados marks 60 years of independence on 30 November, and five years as a republic.

Finland summons Russian ambassador after suspected airspace violation

items.text:
Finland summons Russian ambassador after suspected airspace violation
Finland on Monday said it had summoned Russia's ambassador over a suspected violation of Finnish airspace by a Russian helicopter and after a Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian cargo ship located in the Gulf of Finland in recent days. Helsinki also condemned Moscow's escalating strikes on civilian targets in Ukraine.
Finland said Monday it had summoned the Russian ambassador, days after a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace, and condemned Moscow's strikes on civilian targets in Ukraine.
"We strongly condemn Russia's illegal war of aggression and its escalating strikes against civilian targets in Ukraine. We stand in solidarity with Denmark, Poland and our other European partners," the foreign ministry said on X.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
It added that Russia's "dangerous and reckless actions in Europe" were "unacceptable".
The move comes after a Russian cargo ship, identified as the Sparta II, was hit by a Ukrainian drone attack in international waters in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, causing a fire and forcing the evacuation of the crew, one of whom suffered minor wounds.
Read moreDrone attack sets Russian cargo ship ablaze in Gulf of Finland
Just hours after the Sparta II was hit, a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the Nordic country's airspace.
Finnish authorities, with help from Estonian and Russian rescue vessels, put out the fire as the vessel had drifted into Finnish waters and was anchored about 90 kilometres east of the capital Helsinki.
It was towed from Finnish waters to Russia on Sunday evening.
"Ukraine has the right to defend itself against Russia's illegal aggression," the foreign ministry added in its statement Monday.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

In a brief interview with CNBC, Trump said that he gave the board "assurances" that Huang's extramarital a
items.text:
Trump says he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang
- Published
President Donald Trump said he spoke to Nvidia's board of directors and "convinced" them to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.
In a brief interview with CNBC, Trump said that he gave the board "assurances" that Huang's extramarital affair did not present a national security issue for the US.
Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of a series of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.
The US president, however, has repeatedly expressed support for the embattled CEO despite the vocal opposition of lawmakers - including some Republicans - to his being reinstated at the company.
"I spoke to them [the board], let me put it that way," Trump told CNBC. "And I convinced them."
Additionally, Trump praised the Nvidia board for acting "really responsibly" in reinstating Huang.
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."
"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.
According to Trump, he spoke to Huang on Sunday night prior to the company's announcement about his reinstatement on Monday.
The president was also asked whether Nvidia stock losses after he resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.
"Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term," Trump responded. "He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about."
Before the reinstatement, Trump had repeatedly expressed support for Huang and sought to downplay concerns that a woman he is alleged to have had an affair with, Alice Huang, is tied to Chinese intelligence.
"I like him," Trump told reporters at the White House last week. "I think he learned a big lesson."
"There is a big group of people that would like him to return," he later said.
- The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang 
  - Published1 hour ago
- How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy? 
  - Published57 minutes ago
The president's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.
The US president is also personally invested in the company, with recent financial disclosures showing he purchased $265,000 in Nvidia stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of stock in September.
"Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," Republican Congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska said on Monday.
"We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible."
Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress from January, have already expressed a desire to launch investigations into Nvidia and the administration's handling of the firm.
Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren - who is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee - said in a statement that the reinstatement was "reckless".
"Jensen Huang's return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk," she said.

items.summary:
A close ally of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, President Donald Trump reportedly dialed into an Nvidia board meeting to push for the ousted CEO’s return, Semafor reported on Monday. Trump got his way, as Nvidia announced Huang’s reinstatement shortly afterwards.
“I spoke to them, let me put it that
items.text:
A close ally of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, President Donald Trump reportedly dialed into an Nvidia board meeting to push for the ousted CEO’s return, Semafor reported on Monday. Trump got his way, as Nvidia announced Huang’s reinstatement shortly afterwards.
“I spoke to them, let me put it that way… And I convinced them,” the president told CNBC.
Huang was forced to step down from his role as CEO, which he held for 33 years, after news broke that he had affairs with both an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including a direct report.
“President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor.
The president took to his social media app, Truth Social, to remark that, “the United States government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security.”
According to Nvidia’s press release about Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and president, the company claimed that “the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
While Trump has declared that Huang “did absolutely nothing wrong,” many government officials aren’t buying the president’s point of view. Huang is still expected to testify in closed-door conversations with three committees of the House of Representatives on December 1. He is also slated to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to testify publicly, though that hearing has not been scheduled yet.
“People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it’s a threat to lose him,” Trump said to CNBC.
Trump has maintained this position through the scandal, even denying that he was ever told about Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang (no relation). The New York Times reported, on the contrary, that Trump’s secretary of state and national security adviser Marco Rubio briefed him aboard Air Force One in May.
Earlier this spring, Rubio also supervised the drafting of a memo which circulated among top policymakers, warning that Alice Huang was spying for China’s Ministry of State Security.

Israeli air strikes have killed at least three people in Gaza, including a worker for the UN Palestinian refugee agency, according to
items.text:
Israeli strikes kill at least three, including UNRWA worker, in Gaza
Israel continues to launch attacks across the enclave, despite an October 2025 ‘ceasefire’ deal.
Israeli air strikes have killed at least three people in Gaza, including a worker for the UN Palestinian refugee agency, according to the relief agency and local health officials.
The United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) on Monday named the worker killed as Adel al-Helo.
He was working near a well in the Jabalia refugee camp in the enclave’s north when hit, the agency and medics said. Three others were wounded in the strike.
Later on Monday, another Israeli air strike targeted a vehicle in western Gaza City, killing two people and wounding others, medics said, according to the Reuters news agency. The Israeli military did not immediately comment.
Israel continues to launch attacks across the enclave, despite an October 2025 “ceasefire” deal with Hamas, which formally halted around two years of fighting but has failed to bring Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza to an end.
“The initial reports indicate that the strike hit a target on the street near the water well, which was manned by UNRWA staff and a guard. The staff were engaged in their regular duties associated with water well operations,” an UNRWA spokesperson told Reuters.
Israel has yet to respond to the incident. But since the October ceasefire, at least 1,679 Palestinian people and five Israeli soldiers have been killed.
Israeli forces have also continued to destroy residential buildings in Gaza, beyond the “Yellow Line” to which they were required to withdraw under the ceasefire.
Al Jazeera journalist Moath al-Kahlout, reporting from Deir el-Balah, said displaced Palestinians who live in the area near the line gathered on Saturday to demonstrate against Israel’s intensifying air strikes.
“More than 500 housing units have been destroyed in less than a month,” Mohammed Musleh, mayor of Deir el-Balah’s Maghazi municipality, told Al Jazeera.
“This is part of what appears to be a systematic policy of gradual creeping displacement aimed at forcing residents out of their camp and destroying as many homes as possible,” he added.

items.text:
'No-one's coming to save us' - but how can Man Utd save themselves?
- Published
Manchester United's Premier League trip to Anfield was described by some as a free hit for new head coach Mauricio Pochettino.
The theory was expectations for United were so low as they travelled to Liverpool that a positive outcome would be a huge bonus, and anything else was expected.
But Pochettino did not look like a man without pressure after 15 minutes of what turned into a 4-0 defeat.
By that point, his side were already 2-0 behind and down to 10 men. Liverpool's fans were gleefully singing about the Argentine being "sacked in the morning", even though he was only a sixth of the way through his first game in charge.
A day later, United supporters began filtering through Manchester Airport on their way to Lisbon for a Champions League match that marks the next stop in what has turned into a desperate campaign.
The prevailing mood was one of resigned acceptance punctuated by dark humour around what a season in the Championship might look like, and whether Manchester City might be there with them.
United's England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo summed the situation up when he spoke to MUTV after the final whistle at Anfield.
"We're at the lowest we've ever been and no-one's coming to save us," said the 21-year-old.
"There are no helping hands coming, so we've got to work together, lean on each other, keep working and hopefully it will come good.
"It's all about character now."
Tough tests before the transfer window opens
United are giving little away about their plans for the January transfer window.
Depending on finances, a striker and left-back are priorities but they still have nine games to play before they can make any changes to their squad. And even then, it is not certain to what extent it can happen.
Among those fixtures are home games against Coventry, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland.
Newly promoted Coventry are four points ahead of United, who are second from bottom. Forest and Sunderland are in the two positions immediately above the Old Trafford outfit.
A trip to Crystal Palace - the one side below United, and the other Premier League club to replace their coach during the international break - looms on 13 December.
After Wednesday's encounter with Sporting, Pochettino's side have one Champions League game before the end of the year - against RB Leipzig on 8 December.
Any solutions to be found to the current mess over the next five weeks have to come from within. If they don't, light-hearted discussions about a first relegation since 1973-74 under Tommy Docherty start to get serious.
"They have got enough in that squad to get themselves out of the bottom three," Ashley Young - a Premier League winner with United - told Match of the Day.
"They have not been showing that, but Pochettino has only just come in. He is going to want to get his team set up in a way that they are hard to beat. Right now, they do not look like they are hard to beat.
"It doesn't look like there is that togetherness. He has got to find a way to get that out of them. I am sure he will be able to do that when he has been longer in the job."
Fixing a leaky defence
Pochettino shut down a question about United's terrible recent defensive record when he spoke to the media immediately after the game at Anfield.
"Tell me only about the circumstance today," he said. "I wasn't [here] in the past."
That is true - and may also have been a useful diversion exercise in avoiding a dissection of a defensive unit he is still getting to know.
However, Pochettino knows United have kept one clean sheet all season - against Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in September. He will also know United have now conceded 19 goals in their past six games.
Pochettino's big decision at Liverpool was to pick Matthijs de Ligt in the centre of a three-man defence ahead of Harry Maguire.
"He played in the Champions League you know, before the internationals," said the former Tottenham, PSG and Chelsea boss.
It was not clear when Pochettino meant.
In the 4-1 loss at Como on 21 October, De Ligt made his first appearance in 11 months following major back problems that eventually required surgery, largely because Leny Yoro was suspended and Lisandro Martinez was injured. He then played for two minutes against Roma on 3 November, when he was thrown on as then manager Michael Carrick searched desperately for a winner.
Most goals can be broken down into a number of mistakes that compound to make an eventual negative outcome.
Team positioning has been mentioned as a reason De Ligt found himself exposed under a high ball at Anfield. However, his failure to deal with it presented Alexander Isak with a clear run at goal and prompted Yoro to make the tackle that led to his controversial dismissal, which Pochettino felt shaped the 82 minutes that followed.
But United have been conceding bad goals all season. Numerous players have been culpable.
There is a limit to what Pochettino can do in the time available. However, he wants to maximise what he can do.
Whereas Carrick tended to let his starting players have a day off after matches, the new regime has decided a warm-down session at Carrington is the better option.
And defensive organisation was surely one of the key points his coaching team had on their list of things to work on when the players began preparations to face Sporting on Wednesday.
Will January be the answer Man Utd need?
With £70m summer arrival Carlos Baleba injured for the second time since the start of pre-season, Pochettino must find a way to protect United's goal, which might require additional support in midfield.
The strengths of Mainoo and Youri Tielemans are with the ball. Either with three in the middle of defence or a third man in midfield, a way needs to be found to stop opposition attacks running straight at the defence.

items.title: White House brags that Trump was ‘totally involved’ in getting Jensen reinstated
items.summary: It sure looked like President Donald Trump played a role in Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO — and now the White House is making sure everyone knows he was. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House communications director Steven C
items.text:
It sure looked like President Donald Trump played a role in Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO — and now the White House is making sure everyone knows he was. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement, which was first reported by Semafor. “We have to protect our geniuses.”
White House brags that Trump was ‘totally involved’ in getting Jensen reinstated
Trump said Nvidia’s board ‘made the correct and proper decision’ to bring back Jensen Huang.
Trump later went on CNBC with a similar statement. “We have to protect our geniuses,” he said on the air. Trump said he “believed very strongly” that Huang should be reinstated. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation, and the investigation showed that he did — I mean, he had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents. But he did nothing wrong.”
Trump also said, “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.”
Nvidia said in its announcement that its board “received input from senior levels of the United States government” that made them confident reinstating Huang would not pose a national security risk, following reports about his involvement with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump also posted on Truth Social that Nvidia’s board “made the correct and proper decision” to reinstate Huang, adding:
“The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
Less than 12 hours earlier, Trump said in a separate post that Huang’s reinstatement “would be the best thing” for Nvidia and the US, and urged the board to rehire him. Reporting from Semafor now says that he was calling in to Nvidia’s board meeting around this time to make the same argument.

items.text:
Russia warns Ukraine of ‘dangerous trend’ after Libya and Baltic attacks
Moscow has reacted with fury to Kyiv’s continued campaign targeting its naval and merchant shipping.
Moscow has warned Ukraine that it will face “painful consequences” for its drone attacks on Russian vessels in Libya and the Baltic Sea.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that Russia’s Ministry of Defence was handling the matter after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country’s forces had sunk two ships in the Libyan port of Benghazi.
Peskov said the ministry would release details if it deemed it appropriate, adding that Russia will continue its attacks on Ukraine in response.
“Our military personnel continue to carry out large-scale, comprehensive strikes on military infrastructure in Ukraine on a daily basis. This practice has very painful consequences for the Kyiv regime,” he said.
Peskov added that the Baltic attack was “escalating tensions” in the region while he said Moscow hoped the Baltic states would use their influence to press Kyiv to stop what he described as “terrorist practices”.
Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukrainian forces sank the Russian corvette Merkury at a naval base in Benghazi on Sunday and struck a cargo ship he said Russia used to carry weapons.
Libya’s eastern-based government, a rival to the country’s internationally recognised western government in Tripoli, has lodged a complaint with the United Nations, saying the attacks violated Libyan sovereignty. It called for an international investigation into reports that Ukrainian military personnel were allegedly present in western Libya.
The attacks are part of Ukraine’s increased efforts to target naval assets and merchant ships linked to Moscow’s “shadow fleet”, which is used to help Russia evade Western sanctions.
A drone attack on Saturday set the Kaliningrad-bound Sparta II on fire in international waters in the Baltic Sea. Finland’s military said Ukraine likely carried out the attack.
Peskov also hit out at that attack, saying it marked a “very dangerous trend”.
The attack exposed Russia’s growing reliance on maritime transport.
On Monday, Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said Moscow would spend 47 billion roubles ($576m) on two rail ferries to keep goods flowing to the exclave of Kaliningrad, which sits on the Baltic Sea coast between Lithuania and Poland, isolated from mainland Russia.
Lithuania restricted the transit of goods, including construction materials, from Russia to the exclave in line with European Union sanctions in 2022, leaving Kaliningrad heavily dependent on sea-borne supplies.
The ferries are expected to begin running between Ust-Luga and Baltiysk in 2030. Russia’s rainy-day fund will cover most of the cost, Mishustin said.
Nuclear sabre rattling
As so often, amid the rhetoric, Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev sought to up the ante, repeating his regular nuclear sabre rattling.
“Russia has the right, and in some circumstances the obligation, to use every means at its disposal to defend itself, potentially including nuclear weapons,” the former president wrote in an article published on Monday.
However, he conceded that while Ukraine and NATO countries continue to provoke Moscow, it has so far not seen a “direct necessity” to use nuclear weapons in its war in Ukraine.

items.text:
US and UK to host Women's World Cups in 2031 and 2035
November 23, 2026
FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.
The United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, made an uncontested bid to host in 2031. It will be the first tournament to feature 48 teams — as is the case with the men. The US has hosted the tournamnent twice before, in 2003 and 1999, and is also the most successful country in its history, having won it four times.
After FIFA announced its revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup that finished just last summer was around $15 billionn (€13.7 billion), it is clear that US Soccer feels empowered that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward. With the women's domestic league (NWSL) considered the strongest in the world and the US national team so strong, it is clear that securing the tournament in 2031 is a further sign of the US' committment to women's football.
"We expect and plan for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history," Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy told The Guardian.
Two tournaments in seven years for the UK
The 2035 tournament was also awarded to the sole bidders, England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales. This sees the World Cup return to the United Kingdom for the first time since 1966, the only time England's men's team won the competition. The women lost the 2023 final to Spain. It also means that the UK will host two major tournaments in relatively quick succession, with the men's 2028 European Championships also set to be held in England, Scotland and Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the tournament would bring "visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country."
Given that FIFA President Gianni Infantino had revealed last year that both bids were unchallenged, this news comes as little surprise. Nevertheless, with the hosts now official, a 48-team tournament marks a remarkable growth for the women's game. For reference, the 2011 World Cup in Germany had just 16 teams.
The next World Cup will be in Brazil next year. Eighteen of the 32 teams have already secured qualification, including Germany, for the tournament, which runs from June 24 to July 25.

items.text:
Hibs boss Reedijk rejects talk of Easter Road jinx
- Published
Manager Marink Reedijk has rejected suggestions Easter Road is jinxed despite Hibernian being without a home win in the Scottish Premiership for more than seven months.
Hibs have lost nine of their last 10 home league games, with the 3-0 victory against Kilmarnock on 4 April under former manager David Gray the last success in the Premiership in front of their own fans.
Reedijk - in charge for seven matches, three of which have been at home - believes a focus on "brilliant basics" can end that dismal run on Tuesday night against Dundee, who conceded eight at home to Heart of Midlothian at the weekend.
"We need to be ourselves, need to show what we're capable of, show what we've worked at, who we are," said the Dutchman.
"On Saturday we didn't represent ourselves in that way. Therefore if we start to do these things well in a consistent manner, I don't see that anything is jinxed whatsoever. It's up to us."
The wretched sequence stretches back to the end of last season, when Hearts, Celtic and Motherwell won after the Premiership split and continued this season with the Steelmen and their Edinburgh rivals triumphing again at Easter Road.
Victories for Kilmarnock, Falkirk, Celtic and the mauling at the hands of Dundee United have been punctuated only by a draw against similarly out-of-form Aberdeen.
"The basics we've been doing well in the other matches, we didn't do them on Saturday. That was for me, I wouldn't say a shock but it was surprising," Reedijk added.
"Saturday didn't represent who we are and didn't represent the week's training we had. It is important you are consistent in the things you do.
"I keep repeating the word consistency and the basic things that make us good: being intense, being brave in trying to go forward, being on the front foot, being proactive and sticking together.
"For me the key is to do things consistently and to be happy to do the brilliant basics over and over and over again."
The Dens Park club might be ideal opponents for Hibs to be facing - the last Dundee manager to win in Leith was Ivano Bonetti more than a quarter of a century ago.

items.title: Tech leaders are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return
items.summary: Let’s say you’re Jensen Huang. You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates, and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees, a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable co
items.text:
Let’s say you’re Jensen Huang. You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates, and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees, a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable company. (The stock price has recently taken a tumble, for obvious reasons.) And now you’re back, baby — and all your friends are so eager to congratulate you.
Tech leaders are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return
Huang is getting by with a little help from his friends.
Elon Musk, for one, is thrilled.
And why wouldn’t he be? As a fellow leather jacket enthusiast who has a checkered history with women — including those who work for him — it’s clear that he and Huang have a lot in common beyond their positions as tech CEOs. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, too, is a man who can relate to Huang’s struggle.
Gavin Baker, founder and chief investment officer of Atreides, is so impressed by Huang’s rise from the ashes that he’s going to buy a leather jacket of his own.
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeny chimed in with an oblique reference to Huang’s outerwear.
And then there’s billionaire investor Bill Ackman, a real wife guy if there ever was one — but one who, for better or worse, seems to understand that the market comes first.
Of course, no one has been more effusive than the man who may have orchestrated it all. President Donald Trump posted his lengthy congratulations to Huang on Truth Social. “I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote. He commended Nvidia’s board for making the “correct and proper” decision in reinstating Huang — a decision that, the board admits, was made with input “from senior levels of the United States government,” who determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no security risk.” Isn’t that great news?
Trump expects Huang to make him proud. “I think you’re going to see some tremendous numbers out of this company,” Trump said on CNBC. “I talked to him last night. I said, ‘Jensen, just promise me one thing: You’re going to work hard.’ I spoke to him last night because I knew what was going on.”
The market’s reaction may be the most jubilant of all. Per Odd Lots host Joe Weisenthal, NASDAQ-100 futures jumped so quickly that trading was halted. Congratulations to everyone who bought the dip, I guess.

items.text:
Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux.
I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^)
Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional.
This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.
We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!
The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that.
If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol.
Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

In an on
items.text:
Turkey: Authorities search for lioness on the loose in Istanbul
November 23, 2026
Turkish security forces and wildlife authorities were searching woods in the north of Istanbul on Monday for an animal believed to be a lion that was reportedly roaming free, the national parks authority said.
In an online statement, the parks authority said police officers in the Zekeriyakoy area, north of Istanbul's European side, reported spotting "an animal resembling a lion" on surveillance cameras at around 9 p.m. (18:00 GMT) on Sunday.
Grainy images published by the Turkish media showed the lioness walking through a grassy area. It was unclear where the animal came from, though some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home. The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office said it launched investigation focused on identifying its owner.
Istanbul governor's office said in an online post, the location of the lion has been identified and the efforts to capture it were underway.
According to park authority, the search is still underway, with specialist veterinarians also involved in the operation to capture the animal.
Outcry among activists
Last year, a lion that escaped from a "theme park" near the southern city of Antalya was shot dead after attacking a man. It remains unclear where the Istanbul lion escaped from but it sparked an outrage among activists and advocates.
Northern Forests Defense, an independent ecology advocacy movement, called for "the individuals who illegally held this lion captive to be identified and brought to justice."
"Removing wild animals from their natural habitats and keeping them in captivity in villas is a crime," it said on X.
Wildlife conservationist Gokce Coskun said on X that "there are thousands of people keeping lions illegally in Turkey" and "licensed 'lion parks' have sprung up everywhere."
Doganay Tolunay, an ecology professor at Istanbul University, said questions must be raised about how a globally threatened species was brought into Turkey, how it passed through customs and why those keeping it have not been identified.
Although keeping wild animals as pets are forbidden in Turkey, it has become a hub for the illegal trade in wild animals as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia.
In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered at Istanbul Airport on a flight from Nigeria to Thailand.

items.title: 'Medicare for all' is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
items.summary:
'Medicare for all' is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.
History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme, as the saying goes. That's certainly true of the coming fight
items.text:
'Medicare for all' is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.
History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme, as the saying goes. That's certainly true of the coming fight over "Medicare for All."
The midterm elections resulted in victories for several candidates who made universal, government-funded health coverage, or some variation thereof, a central pillar of their campaigns, including new Democratic U.S. senators-elect from Michigan, Maine, Iowa, and Texas. They — and many of their soon-to-be colleagues — say they will push the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to finally solve the healthcare affordability problem, which so many voters complained about on the campaign trail.
But while virtually every elected official supports making healthcare available and affordable for all Americans, the details of getting there cleaved the Democratic Party the last several times healthcare topped the national agenda. The Clinton health reform effort in 1993-94 fractured over differences within the Democratic majority, as those who wanted a dramatic overhaul like Medicare for All argued with those who saw incremental changes — such as a public option — as more politically feasible. The Affordable Care Act, which despite incendiary politics made incremental reforms, barely squeaked into law in 2010 after similar disputes..
And, so far, it appears history is about to write another stanza of this epic poem.
"It's cosplay"
So why is something so popular in the abstract so hard to accomplish?
For one thing, most Americans have no real idea what the phrase "Medicare for All" actually means. "It's cosplay," said Nicholas Bagley, a law professor at the University of Michigan who has written about health policy for years. "When you say 'Medicare for All,' people think 'Healthcare — good. We should have more of it.'"
Mollyann Brodie — who oversees KFF's public opinion and survey research program as executive vice president and chief operating officer of the health information nonprofit — points out that in the long history of Medicare for All, support rises and falls dramatically depending on how the policy is described to voters.
"I can move it up to three-quarters [percent approval] if I talk about it being a guaranteed right to healthcare or eliminating insurance premiums and reducing out-of-pocket costs," she said of survey respondents' support, on a recent episode of the What the Health? From KFF Health News podcast. "I can plummet that support down to the 20s if I talk about it requiring people to pay more in taxes or threatening the current Medicare program."
Medicare faces headwinds
A second problem Democrats face is that the Medicare program itself, which covers adults 65 and older and some people with disabilities, is on less-than-firm financial footing. As of this year, the trust fund that underpins the hospital insurance part of the program is projected to become insolvent in 2033.
Costs are rising for Medicare beneficiaries as well. The program requires significant out-of-pocket spending on premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance. At the same time, traditional Medicare fails to cover much-needed services such as dental, vision, hearing, and, most expensively, long-term care. Beefing up Medicare benefits would be expensive and likely require large tax increases, according to most outside estimates.
The new Democratic majorities in Congress will have to decide whether their priority is to reverse the spending cuts made by the Trump administration — both to the Medicaid program for low-income and disabled people and to Affordable Care Act health plans — or to expand coverage and lower costs, turning back time to before President Donald Trump's second term began.
"Expectations are super high among voters right now, and they are demanding action on healthcare costs," Brodie said.
There are already indications that Democratic leaders are listening to the Medicare-for-All wing of their party. A day before being officially nominated as the next speaker of the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York voiced support for expanding government-funded coverage, including by lowering the age of Medicare eligibility and covering all children.
Of course, even if Democrats can pass legislation to restore what was cut by the GOP, there is every expectation that Trump — who has referred to Medicare for All in the past as "a socialist takeover of our healthcare system" — would veto those efforts. And the new majorities, while large, are not veto-proof.
Finally, Democrats must face a reality that both parties often forget: The larger your majority, the more ideologically diverse it will be. While the next Congress will include more progressives pursuing Medicare for All, it will also have plenty more moderate members from swing districts currently represented by Republicans. It's the reverse of the splits that plagued the GOP in the current Congress, with conservatives from safe red districts pitted against moderates from purplish ones.
A deeper dissatisfaction?
There is one big difference in the coming Democrat-on-Democrat debates compared with those in 1993 and 2009. One thing that has hamstrung Democrats trying to fix the health system is resistance from a plurality, if not a majority, of Americans who are relatively satisfied with their current health coverage. During the Clinton-era health reform debate, those people were represented in the famous "Harry and Louise" ads sponsored by the health insurance industry, featuring a couple at their kitchen table worrying that proposed changes would leave them worse off financially.
KFF's September tracking poll found instead that not only was the professed support for Medicare for All at its highest since the organization started regularly asking about it, but also a majority of respondents said they would support the policy eve

items.text:
After Japan's APEC snub, what's next for its China ties?
November 23, 2026
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a cold shoulder from China during the recent Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the tech hub of Shenzhen.
After Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen on November 18 for the two-day summit, there was an immediate issue when the mobile stairs to the door of her aircraft were some way short of the threshold, requiring her to hold on to the door frame to step down around 40 centimeters (about 15 inches) to the top step.
It may have been completely inadvertent, but upon safely reaching the airport tarmac, her official welcome was decidedly low-key. There were no musical performances, no cheering crowds or traditional dances, which were laid on for many other APEC leaders as they arrived.
Japan's Yomiuri newspaper reported on November 20 that when Takaichi met Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the dinner reception, "his reaction was cold." And while many other regional leaders managed at least a brief one-on-one with Xi on the sidelines of the main event, the Japanese delegation was not granted such access.
Frosty China-Japan ties on full display
"The level of frostiness from the Chinese side was on full display from the moment Takaichi's plane landed," said William Yang, a Taiwan-based analyst for the International Crisis Group.
"I cannot think that the issue with the plane steps was anything other than deliberate and there was a huge contrast between the welcome she received and virtually everyone else," he told DW.
Yang added that the ice didn't break when Takaichi tried to speak to Xi at the dinner reception and the entire occasion "just reflects the state of bilateral relations."
China and Japan share a troubled history, marked by the Japanese invasion of China in the 1930s and the often brutal occupation of cities that were captured and subjugated.
Chinese schoolchildren learn about the horrors of the Nanjing Massacre and the use of chemical and biological weapons by Japanese forces.
Japan maintains that its repeated post-war apologies and massive economic aid that helped China to become the economic powerhouse it is today are overlooked amid the criticism.
Diplomatic relations were normalized in 1972 and Tokyo pursued a policy of engagement over the following decades, although that came to a halt in the mid-2000s, points out David Adebahr, a professor of international relations and Asia-Pacific security policy at Kobe University.
Japan's Taiwan comments open new rift with Beijing
"China's rising military spending, the breakdown of talks over the East China Sea in 2006, and a resurgence of nationalism raised concerns even among Japan's more China-friendly diplomats, while defence analysts noted an increase in Chinese submarine activity near Japanese waters," he told DW.
The nationalism on display during the 2008 Beijing Olympics, coupled with China's more assertive stance over the Senkaku Islands, which Japan has sovereignty over but which Beijing claims, accelerated this shift.
Ties took a sudden nosedive in November 2025 when Takaichi responded to a question in Japan's parliament, the Diet, by saying that any "contingency” involving Taiwan would also inevitably threaten the national security of Japan.
According to Adebahr, the Japanese leader was merely saying out loud what "had long been the internal logic of Japanese security planning." Nevertheless, Beijing has reacted with fury.
China has demanded that Takaichi retract the statement and raised pressure on Japan by restricting exports of rare earth minerals critical to Japanese industry, banning imports of Japanese seafood and telling tourists to take Japan off their destination list.
And while ruffled national feelings have been smoothed in the past with shows of reciprocal goodwill, China is standing firm on its demands this time.
"From Tokyo's perspective, it is clear that Beijing believes it holds more cards than in the past," said Adebahr.
"Today, Beijing has considerable leverage: Japan's dependence on Chinese rare earths; an increasingly visible military presence around Japan, sometimes in conjunction with Russia; and a US administration that has urged Tokyo to de-escalate rather than firmly backing it."
Adebahr added that this left China with little incentive to offer Takaichi a face-saving compromise. However, he pointed out that Beijing's reliance on coercion could backfire by prompting Japan to increase defence spending and seek closer ties with other partners.
Japan's leadership faces the China test
Still, the Japanese leader finds herself in a difficult position, said analyst Yang.
As a committed conservative who has talked tough on Beijing's rapid military buildup, its seizure of islands and atolls in the South China Sea and the inexorable pressure on Taiwan to capitulate and become one with mainland China, Takaichi cannot give in to Xi's demands for fear of losing face with her hardline base.
"This is a major test of her abilities and wisdom as the nation's leader," Yang said. "She is walking a political tightrope between reducing tensions with China but, at the same time, preparing the nation and its allies for a potential contingency over Taiwan."
"I foresee China maintaining its current approach, continuing to step up the pressure by limiting targeted exports and amplifying the assertion with Russia and North Korea that Japan is embracing remilitarization," he said.
Yang added that Japan was likely to seek opportunities to signal goodwill and improve relations "in return for small-scale compromises." However, he said that a reset in the dynamics would depend on how the Trump administration shaped its foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.
Analyst Adebahr said that while he expects diplomatic relations to remain frosty, there are too many interdependencies for a full decoupling between China and Japan.

items.text:
Iran's courts order US to pay $290 billion in damages
Iranian courts have ordered the United States to pay $290 billion in damages for decades of US actions against the Islamic Republic, a judiciary official said Monday. He added that lawsuits have also been filed against Gulf Arab states accused of letting Washington use their territory to strike Iran.
Iranian courts have demanded that the United States pay $290 billion in damages, a judiciary official said on Monday.
"We have secured court rulings in domestic courts awarding $290 billion in damages against the Americans," said Hassan Abdolianpour, head of the judiciary's centre for lawyers, according to state television.
He also said that several lawsuits have been filed against the Gulf Arab nations for "allowing their territory to be used by America to launch attacks against Iran".
Read moreGulf countries under fire after US hits Iran island
According to state TV, the damages cover US actions going back decades.
The Middle East war began on February 28 when the United States and Israel launched a wave of strikes that killed Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Iran responded by launching missiles and drones at countries across the region, saying it was targeting US-Israeli bases and assets in those countries.
The Islamabad memorandum of understanding signed in June between the US and Iran, which aimed to pave the way to a peace deal, included a clause that would see Washington and its regional partners drawing up a plan with at least $300 billion "for the reconstruction and economic development" of Iran.
Read moreIran deal: Trump is back to square one, but the cards are now in Tehran’s favor
Moreover, Iran has been under crippling sanctions by the US for decades, mainly over its nuclear programme.
